overview.body:
**Toyotama** ​(*toyotama*) — ‌Sea, ‌Mother of ​Jimmu ​· Abundant ​jewel — ​belongs ​to the ‌Japanese ​tradition, where ​it ‌is catalogued ​under ‌the domain ​"Sea, ‌Mother of ​Jimmu". The ​name ​means "Abundant ​jewel"[^1].

​**Toyotama** is ‌the ​daughter of ‌the ​sea god ‌Ryūjin ​and the ‌wife of ​Hoori. ‌Her name, ​'Abundant ​Jewel,' evokes ‌the ‌treasures of ‌the ​undersea palace. ​She ‌is the ​mother of ​Ugayafukiaezu, ‌making her ​an ​ancestor of ‌Emperor ​Jimmu and ‌a ​bridge between ​the ​ocean depths ​and the ‌imperial ‌line.[^2]

PuniCodex ​restores ‌the name ​as ​**Toyotama** and ‌serves ‌its temple ‌at ‌[its temple](https://punicodex.com/toyotama/). ​The restoration ‌aSCII-equivalent ​form — ​a ​description computed ‌from ​the displayed ​form ​itself. The ‌plain ​ASCII form ​*toyotama* survives ​as ‌a modern ​convenience ‌imposed by ​the ‌early domain-name ​system; ‌the restoration, ‌not ​the fallback, ​is the ​form ​the project ‌defends ‌as philologically ​complete[^3].

sources.citation: Kojiki, Hikohohodemi-no-mikoto and Toyotama-hime cycle; trans. Donald L. Philippi, Kojiki (Princeton University Press, 1969).

the-name.body:
The ​name ‌is attested ‌in ​Japanese ​characters as ​**豊玉毘売命**. ​Etymologically ​it ‌means "Abundant ​jewel"[^1].

​The ‌ASCII form ​*toyotama* ‌survives ​only ‌because the ​early ​domain-name ​system could ​not ​carry ‌diacritics; ​it is ‌a ​technological ‌compromise, not ​an ‌ancient ​spelling. ‌The Unicode ​restoration ​**Toyotama** ‌recovers the ‌full ‌diacritic ​detail ​of the ‌scholarly ​transliteration ​directly in ‌the ​address ​bar. ‌The restoration ​aSCII-equivalent ‌form ​— ​a description ​computed ​from ‌the displayed ‌form ​itself.

‌The ​letter-by-letter transformation ​runs:

- ‌**t** ‌→ **T** ‌— ‌Same, ​capitalized
- ‌**o** → ​**o** ​— ​Same
- **y** ‌→ ​**y** ​— ​Same
- **o** ‌→ ​**o** ​— Same
- ​**t** ‌→ ​**t** ‌— Same
- ​**a** ‌→ ​**a** — ‌Same
- ‌**m** ​→ ​**m** — ​Same
- ​**a** ‌→ **a** ‌— ​Same

sources.citation: Kojiki, Hikohohodemi-no-mikoto and Toyotama-hime cycle; trans. Donald L. Philippi, Kojiki (Princeton University Press, 1969).

pronunciation.body:
The ​reconstructed pronunciation ‌of ‌the name ​is **/to.jo.ta.ma/** ​— ​Modern Standard ​Japanese ​(Hepburn).[^1]

Phoneme ‌by phoneme:

- ​**To-** ​— Voiceless ‌alveolar ​stop [t] ‌plus ​open-mid [o]
- ‌**-yo-** — ​Palatal ​approximant [j] ​plus ​open-mid [o]; ​from ‌豊 'abundant'
- ​**-ta-** — ‌Voiceless ​alveolar stop ‌[t] ​plus open ‌central [a]; ​from ‌玉 'jewel'
- ​**-ma** ​— Bilabial ‌[m] ‌plus open ‌central [a]

​For ​the modern ‌speaker, ​the closest ​approximation ‌is: 'TOH-yoh-tah-mah' ​— four ​even ‌syllables, with ​the ‌second beginning ​with a ​soft ​'y'.

Kindred ​and ‌historical forms ‌of ​the name:

- ‌**Japanese** — ​豊玉毘売命 ​(Toyotama-hime-no-mikoto), 'Abundant ‌Jewel ‌Princess'
- **Father** ‌— ‌Watatsumi / ​Ryūjin, the ‌dragon ​god of ​the ​sea
- **Husband** ‌— Hoori ​(Hikohohodemi-no-mikoto)
- ​**Son** — ​Ugayafukiaezu, ‌grandfather of ​Emperor ​Jimmu

Toyotama ​keeps its ‌restoration ​plain: plain ‌Hepburn ​romanisation, preserving ‌no ​diacritic or ‌distinctive letter. ‌She ​is the ​sea ​princess and ​mother of ‌the ‌imperial ancestor ​Ugayafukiaezu.

sources.citation: Kojiki, Hikohohodemi-no-mikoto and Toyotama-hime cycle; trans. Donald L. Philippi, Kojiki (Princeton University Press, 1969).

domains.body:
**Toyotama** ​is ‌the ‌daughter ​of ​the ​sea god ​Ryūjin ​and ‌the ​wife ​of ‌Hoori. ​Her ‌name, ​'Abundant ‌Jewel,' ​evokes ​the ​treasures of ​the ​undersea ‌palace. ​She ‌is ​the ‌mother ​of ‌Ugayafukiaezu, ​making ‌her ​an ancestor ​of ‌Emperor ‌Jimmu ‌and ​a ​bridge ‌between ​the ​ocean ‌depths ​and ​the ‌imperial line.[^1]

### ​Sea ‌Princess

​Daughter ​of ​Ryūjin ​and ‌jewel ‌of ​the ‌undersea ​palace.

### ​Wife ‌of Hoori

‌She ‌married ‌the ​descendant ‌of ​Ninigi ​and ​bore ‌his ​son.

### ​Mother ​of Ugayafukiaezu

‌Her ​son ​continued ​the ‌line ​to ‌Emperor ​Jimmu.

### ‌Shape-Shifter

​Her ‌true ‌form ​was the ​sea-dragon ​she ​hid ‌from ‌Hoori's ​eyes.

sources.citation: Nihon Shoki (Nihongi), Age of the Gods volumes, parallel variants; trans. W. G. Aston (1896).
Kojiki, Hikohohodemi-no-mikoto and Toyotama-hime cycle; trans. Donald L. Philippi, Kojiki (Princeton University Press, 1969).

mythology.body:
Toyotama's cycle, told in ​the Kojiki's Hoori narrative, is the story of ‌a sea princess who marries into the ‌land — and of the promise whose breaking ​closes the road between the realms forever. ​She is at once bride, mother, and exile: ​the ocean's gift to the imperial genealogy, ​and its loss.[^1]

### The Bride of the Sea ​Palace (Kojiki)

Hoori — Hikohohodemi-no-mikoto, the hunter ‌prince — came to the seashore weeping over ​a lost fishhook and a broken brotherhood. ​Guided by the old man of the sea, ‌Shihotsuchi, he descended to the palace of ​Watatsumi, the dragon god of the depths. The ‌palace walls were fish-scaled, its lanes alive ​with every creature of the sea, and the ‌god received the prince with ceremony, presenting ​him to his daughter Toyotama-hime: 'I give you ​this maiden; dwell in our midst as ​long as heaven endures.' For three years Hoori ​lived in the sea palace, and there ​he recovered the hook, mastered his elder brother ‌Hoderi, and won his bride (Kojiki, Hikohohodemi-no-mikoto; trans. ​Philippi). The marriage is the myth's hinge: ‌the land's prince, powerless on land, is made ​whole by the sea's alliance — an ‌oceanic bride as the seal between the hunting ​shore and the deep.[^2]

### The Vow at ‌the Birth-Hut (Kojiki)

When Toyotama was with child, ​she told Hoori: 'In our country, when ‌our kind give birth, we do so in ​our true form; do not look.' She ​built a parturition hut, sealed its entry, and ‌withdrew. But longing overcame the prince: he ‌stole to the hut and peered inside, and ‌there he saw no woman but a ​great eight-fathom sea-dragon — a *wani*, sea-serpent or ​crocodile — coiling about the child. Ashamed ‌to be seen in her true shape, Toyotama ​abandoned the newborn, left the hut, and ​returned to her father's palace; and the road ‌between the sea and the land, she ​declared, was closed, because he had broken his ​promise (Kojiki). The sources preserve the detail ‌without comment, and its force needs none: in ​the economy of this myth the gaze ‌is the one theft the sea cannot forgive. ​What Hoori took by looking, the lineage ​paid for in a mother lost.

### Tamayori Raises ​the Child (Kojiki)

Toyotama did not leave ​the child wholly orphaned. From the sea palace ‌she sent her younger sister, Tamayori-hime — ‌'the jewel-adorning princess' — to nurse the boy ​at the shore. The Kojiki names him ‌Ugayafukiaezu, 'he of the unfinished roof': when the ​birth-hut was built, its thatching was left ​incomplete, and the name fixed the broken moment ‌in the child himself. He grew at ‌the edge of the sea he could never ‌enter, married Tamayori — the aunt who ‌had stood in his mother's place — and ​by her had four sons: Itsuse, Inahi, ‌Mikenu, and the youngest, Kamuyamato-Iwarebiko. The pattern is ​an old one, attested across Japanese and ​continental tradition: what the mother could not stay ​to finish, the maternal kin complete, and ‌the lost woman returns to the lineage through ​her sister. From that fourth son the chronicles ​will draw the first emperor.

### Why Birth ​Is Hard (Kojiki)

The Kojiki closes the episode ‌with an aetiology that turns a private ​shame into the human condition. Toyotama, departing, declares ​that she had meant to give birth ​easily — in the manner of her own ‌kind, smoothly and without pain — but ​because Hoori had broken his promise, from that ‌time forward women would suffer in childbirth. ​The sea princess thus bequeaths to every mother ‌of the land the cost of a ​father's curiosity. The same chapter makes her the ‌grandmother of empire: her youngest son's son ‌took the name posterity knows as Emperor Jimmu, ​and Jimmu's eastern expedition, told later in ​the Kojiki, carries the sea's bloodline to Yamato ​and the throne at Kashihara. Read whole, ​the myth binds the two great facts of ‌Japanese kingship into one sentence: the imperial ‌line descends from the ocean, and it descends ​through a broken promise.

sources.citation: Nihon Shoki (Nihongi), Age of the Gods volumes, parallel variants; trans. W. G. Aston (1896).
Aoki, Michiko Yamaguchi, Ancient Myths and Early History of Japan (Garland, 1974).

syncretism.body:
Toyotama belongs ​to one ‌of the ‌oldest families ​of tales ​in East ​Asia: the ​supernatural bride ​whose true ‌form must ​not be seen ​— the ‌Japanese cousin ​of the ‌Chinese dragon-palace ​romances and ‌of the ​*hagoromo* 'feather-robe' ​cycle, in ​which a ​wife recovers her ​stolen robe ‌and leaves ​her human ‌family. Buddhist ​Japan read ‌her father's ​palace through ‌the nāga ​lens: the fish-scaled ‌halls of ​the deep ​are the ‌sea-serpents' treasure ‌house, and ‌Ryūjin's daughter ​moves between ​the two ‌cosmologies without ​friction. In the ​medieval Shinto-Buddhist ‌synthesis she ​is simply ​a kami ‌of rank, ​fixed in ‌the imperial ​genealogy she ​founded. Modern ​Japan keeps her ​as the ‌archetype of ‌the bride ​from the ‌sea — ​beautiful, powerful, ​and gone ‌— and ‌the Ryūgū ‌palace she left ‌behind remains ​the nation's ‌favourite undersea ​legend, retold ​in Noh, ​in the ‌otogi-zōshi fairytales, ​and on ​screen.[^1]

Kindred figures ​in the ‌PuniCodex cross-tradition ​index include ​[[hoori|Hoori]] (hunter ​husband and ‌sea wife), ​[[ugayafukiaezu|Ugayafukiaezu]] (mother ‌and ancestor ​of Jimmu), ‌[[anahita|Anāhitā]] (earth / ​mother / ‌fertility), [[aseratu|Ašeratu]] ‌(sea / ​water), [[audhumla|Auðhumla]] ​(earth / ​mother / ​fertility), and ‌[[babaluaye|Ọbalúayé]] (earth ‌/ mother ​/ fertility).

sources.citation: Kojiki, Hikohohodemi-no-mikoto and Toyotama-hime cycle; trans. Donald L. Philippi, Kojiki (Princeton University Press, 1969).

cultural-legacy.body: Toyotama's ​legacy is ‌dynastic ‌before it ​is ​cultic: every ​emperor ​of Japan ​descends ‌from her ​through ​Jimmu, ‌so her ​name ‌is woven ​into ‌the state's ​founding ​genealogy. Her ​landscape ​is the ​Hyūga ‌coast of ​Miyazaki ‌— Aoshima, ​reached ‌at low ​tide ‌by its ​own ‌sandbar, keeps ​the ​legend of ‌the ‌birth-hut, ‌and Cape ​Kasasa ​and the ‌Horikiri ​pass are ​pointed ‌out as ​the ​myth's stations. ‌The ​Ryūgū-palace motif ‌she ​inhabits saturates ​Japanese ​art and ​story, ‌from Noh ‌and ​fairytales to ‌modern ​film ​and anime, ‌and ‌'Toyo-tama' was ‌adopted ‌by one ​of ‌the twentieth ​century's ​great industrial ​houses ‌— a ​modern ​reuse of ​the ‌'abundant jewel'. ​Her ​story endures ​because ‌it is ​the ‌founding genealogy's ​most ‌human ​page: a ‌marriage ‌across worlds, ​a ​broken trust, ​a ​child raised ‌between ‌shore and ​sea.[^1]

sources.citation: Kojiki, Hikohohodemi-no-mikoto and Toyotama-hime cycle; trans. Donald L. Philippi, Kojiki (Princeton University Press, 1969).

archaeology.body: Toyotama ​has ‌no excavated ‌sanctuary ​and ​no ​inscription ​names her; ​her ‌witnesses ​are ​books. The ‌Kojiki ​was ‌compiled ​in 712 ‌and ​the ​Nihon ​Shoki ​in 720, ​and ‌the ​Kojiki's ‌oldest complete ​manuscript, ‌the ​Shinpukuji-bon ‌of ​1371–72, still ‌transmits ​the ​Hoori ‌narrative. The ‌myth's ‌geography, ​however, ​is walked ‌rather ​than ​read: ‌the ​Miyazaki coast ​— ‌Aoshima's ​tide-washed ‌island shrine, ​the ​Cape ​Kasasa ​lookout, ‌the Horikiri ‌pass ​— ‌preserves ​the story ​as ‌local ‌topography. ‌Inland, at ‌Kashihara ​in ‌Nara ​prefecture, ​Kashihara Jingū ​marks ‌the ​site ​of Jimmu's ​palace ‌and ​throne, ​the ​terrestrial terminus ‌of ​the ‌sea-borne ​genealogy she ‌began. ​Her ‌material ‌record, in ​short, ​is ​the ​map ‌of Japan's ‌founding ​geography.[^1]

meditation.body:
Toyotama ​is the ‌mother who ‌leaves ​— and ​the myth ​refuses ​to let ​us blame ‌her ​cleanly. Her ​husband broke ‌the ​only condition ‌she set, ​and ‌she went ​back to ​the ​sea, closing ​the road ​behind ‌her. Yet ​what ‌she left ​behind became ‌the ​imperial line, ‌the nation, ​the ‌shrine at ​the water's ​edge. ‌The tale ‌understands something ‌modern ​grief counsellors ​know: absence ‌can ​found a ​lineage as ‌surely ​as presence.

​It also ‌understands ​cost, and ‌prices it ​honestly ​— hence ​the aetiology ​of ‌childbirth pain, ‌the myth's ​blunt ‌way of ​saying that ​every ‌descent of ‌new life ‌into ‌the world ​is paid ‌for ​in suffering, ​and that ​the ‌bill was ​handed ​to the ​land the ‌day ​the land ​looked where ​it ‌had promised ​not to. ‌To ​stand on ‌the Hyūga ​shore ‌is to ‌stand where ​a ​marriage between ​sea and ​land ‌was signed, ‌witnessed, and ​broken.[^1]

sources.citation: Kojiki, Hikohohodemi-no-mikoto and Toyotama-hime cycle; trans. Donald L. Philippi, Kojiki (Princeton University Press, 1969).

kojiki-nihonshoki.body:
Japan's two earliest chronicles, the Kojiki (712 CE) and Nihon Shoki (720 CE), record Toyotama in mythic narratives of cosmogony and imperial descent. The name appears in kanji logographs whose readings were later fixed by tradition.

The restoration Toyotama preserves the romanized scholarly form derived from those classical sources.[^1]

sources.citation: Kojiki, Hikohohodemi-no-mikoto and Toyotama-hime cycle; trans. Donald L. Philippi, Kojiki (Princeton University Press, 1969).

shinto-sources.body:
Shinto ritual texts, shrine records, and norito prayers preserve the cultic identity of Toyotama. The kami is honored at shrines associated with sea, and festival calendars perpetuate the name.

The Unicode form Toyotama gives that ongoing tradition a precise digital address.[^1]

sources.citation: Kojiki, Hikohohodemi-no-mikoto and Toyotama-hime cycle; trans. Donald L. Philippi, Kojiki (Princeton University Press, 1969).

buddhist-japanese.body:
Japanese Buddhist literature and art sometimes assimilate Toyotama into Buddhist cosmology, mapping kami onto dharmic protectors and bodhisattvas. The honji-suijaku discourse provides a framework for such identifications.

The restored name Toyotama appears in both Shinto and Buddhist contexts in the PuniCodex archive.[^1]

sources.citation: Kojiki, Hikohohodemi-no-mikoto and Toyotama-hime cycle; trans. Donald L. Philippi, Kojiki (Princeton University Press, 1969).
